centered-cloud.t: Here are the six centered customers. **Which axis through the center captures the most spread?** We will try different directions and measure each one.

candidate-axis.t: The yellow line is a candidate axis at **135°**, running against the trend. The graph on the right will track the variance along the axis as we turn it.

project-points.t: Each customer is dropped perpendicularly onto the axis. The small dots on the line are the **projected positions**, and their spread is what we measure.

small-spread.t: The projections bunch tightly together: the variance is only **0.20**, the lowest point on the curve. This axis throws away most of the spread in the data.

rotate-axis.t: As the axis turns to **90°** (the spend axis), the projections spread out and the variance rises to **2.70**. The pink dot slides along the curve.

larger-spread.t: Turning toward the trend, to **60°**, raises the variance to **5.41**. The green bar along the axis shows the points spreading out.

maximum-spread.t: Near **41°** the curve peaks: the variance reaches about **6.03**. Turning further would reduce it again, so this is the direction of greatest spread.

first-direction.t: That best axis is **PC1 = (0.754, 0.657)**, with variance **6.03**. The arrow points along the cloud and is a mix of both original features.

orthogonal-second.t: **PC2** is perpendicular to PC1 (the small square marks the right angle) and captures what is left: variance **0.17**. In two dimensions it is fixed once PC1 is chosen.

principal-directions.t: The two perpendicular axes, ordered by variance (**6.03 and 0.17**), add up to the original total of **6.20**. Rotating the axes reorganizes the spread but does not change it.
